newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - BA/AA deal seen hurting Virgin's profits.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - BA/AA deal seen hurting Virgin's profits.

text.p: Richard Branson, colorful British entreprenuer and outspoken opponent of the proposed British Airways and American Airlines alliance, said a deal between the two carriers would hurt Virgin Atlantic Airways' expansion and profits.
"It will curtail our expansion. It will curtail our profits," he told Reuters in an interview Wednesday.
"But until we know what form it comes out in - if it comes out at all - it's difficult to be more precise," Branson said.
On a press junket to tout his position that the BA-American deal would stifle competition and raise fares for consumers, Branson said he doubts regulators will approve the alliance.
"We believe we can stop it. In the end, we don't believe the governments - the Clinton adminstration or the British government - would allow such a merger to take place," he said.
Even if the alliance were approved, Branson said he was comfortable with estimates for turnaround of 900 million pounds and profits of about 65-70 million stg for the year ending August 1997.
"The effects of any alliance would not take place for another 12 months or so, so it would not affect those numbers" Branson said.
Branson suggested that allowing BA and American to join forces would be as absurd as allowing Coke and Pepsi to merge.

Even if the carriers agreed to consessions, such as reducing their hold on the majority of slots at London's Heathrow Airport, Branson said the power of the two airlines would be lethal to the travel industry.

"The power that they will have over the travel trade, the power over corporate entities and over frequent flier programs would be such that...they'd still be a real threat to other airlines and dictate prices for the consumer," Branson said.
For consumers to see any real benefits in selection and fares, Branson said regulators must pursue broader "open skies" aviation treaties.
The current aviation talks between the United States and Britain are merely a piecemeal attempt to liberate aviation pacts, Branson said.

"This hybrid open skies that some of the official talk about goes absolutely against what the Western world stands for. Any compromise to total open skies should just not happen. It's archaic. It's antiquated. "
Instead of negotiating aviation agreements one country at time, Branson suggests that barriers should be removed throughout the U.S. and Europe.

"Open skies must mean open skies. It must mean that Southwest Airlines should be able to fly anywhere in Europe, fly across the Atlantic and fly anywhere in America," Branson said. "And open skies would mean that Virgin Atlantic and Virgin Express could do the same."

"The benefit of that to the consumer would be enormous," he said. "In any other business - car manufacturing, soft drinks, the record industry - there are no boundaries. Why should the airline business be any different.
Branson said the open skies pact previously reached between the U.S. and Germany is biased towards American carriers.
"It's an American version of open skies," he said.

The fate of the BA and American alliance remains in the hands of regulators. U.S. officials maintain that approval of the deal is contingent on first securing an Anglo-U.S. aviation pact that would give U.S. carriers access to London's Heathrow Airport.
American Airline's chief executive Robert Crandall said Tuesday that slow progress in the open skies talks would likely mean a delay in implementing the deal by the April 1997 target date.
-- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610
